analysis.one_liner: Makes it much harder for big companies to merge, outspend rivals, and force consumers into arbitration over antitrust claims.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee since January 2025 with no hearing, no markup, and no vote; all 13 cosponsors are Democrats, and Republicans who hold 55 Senate seats have shown no support.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill rewrites the nation's antitrust laws to make it easier for the government to stop big mergers. Today, the government must prove a merger would substantially harm competition; this bill would block any merger that creates an appreciable risk of material harm, including deals that let one company or employer dominate a market and push down wages or supplier prices. For very large deals, the companies would have to prove the merger is harmless rather than the government proving it is harmful. It also bans dominant firms from certain exclusionary conduct, adds penalties tied to a company's revenue, bars companies from forcing antitrust disputes into arbitration, protects whistleblowers who report price-fixing, and boosts funding for the Justice Department and FTC antitrust enforcers.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and small businesses who face higher prices from concentrated industries; workers in labor markets dominated by a few large employers, where monopsony power has been shown to hold down wages; suppliers and franchises squeezed by dominant buyers; antitrust whistleblowers reporting price-fixing; and plaintiffs who want their day in court instead of forced arbitration. Federal antitrust enforcers also gain funding and new tools.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, workers, and small businesses facing concentrated markets

how_it_helps.text: It replaces today's 'substantially lessen competition' test with a stricter one: a merger is unlawful if it creates an 'appreciable risk of materially lessening competition,' and it makes mergers that tend to create a monopsony — a dominant employer or buyer that can push down wages or supplier prices — a violation of the Clayton Act.

It shifts the burden of proof to the merging companies for very large deals — acquisitions over $5 billion, or any deal over $50 million involving a company with $100 billion or more in assets, sales, or market value — so the companies must prove the deal will not hurt competition rather than the government proving it will.

It makes it unlawful for dominant firms (generally over 50 percent market share) to engage in exclusionary conduct that risks harming competition, backed by civil penalties of up to 15 percent of the company's U.S. revenues, and adds similar revenue-based penalties for Sherman Act violations.

It bars companies from using pre-dispute arbitration clauses or class-action waivers in antitrust disputes, so consumers and small businesses can join together in a class action in court instead of being forced into individual arbitration.
It protects employees and contractors who report antitrust violations from retaliation and creates whistleblower rewards of 10 to 30 percent of criminal fines over $1 million.

It adds a Competition Advocate inside the FTC with its own subpoena power, a Market Analysis and Data office, a required GAO study of how mergers affect wages, employment, innovation, and new business formation, a study of large institutional investors' overlapping stakes in competitors, and increased funding for the DOJ Antitrust Division and the FTC.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations and dominant firms in concentrated industries, which would face far greater odds of having mergers blocked, exclusionary practices challenged, and penalties up to 15 percent of U.S. revenues; private equity and big acquirers facing higher transaction costs; and the arbitration industry, which loses antitrust cases it currently channels out of court.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large dominant corporations and big acquirers

drawbacks.text: The new standard bars mergers that merely pose an 'appreciable risk' of materially lessening competition — a much lower bar than today's 'substantial' harm test. Critics, including business groups and some economists, argue this would deter efficient mergers that genuinely lower costs or accelerate innovation, since companies would not know in advance whether a deal could survive.

Large acquirers would bear the burden of proving a deal is lawful, with thresholds that capture any acquisition above $5 billion and any big deal by a company over $100 billion in size. That shifts review costs to dealmakers and could slow legitimate acquisitions of startups that depend on being bought.

Civil penalties of up to 15 percent of a company's total U.S. revenues — potentially tens of billions of dollars for the largest firms — are an aggressive deterrent that businesses argue could exceed the actual harm in a case.

A presumption of liability for exclusionary conduct by any firm with more than 50 percent market share could sweep in aggressive-but-legal competitive conduct, such as steep price cuts or bundled offerings, forcing dominant firms to defend routine business strategies in court.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets real harms: concentrated industries have used their market position to raise prices and suppress wages, and forced arbitration has made it hard for consumers and small businesses to band together to sue. A stricter merger standard, monopsony protections, and penalties scaled to company revenue would give enforcers real teeth. The honest costs are that the new standard is deliberately broader than current law, so courts would have to sort out which mergers genuinely help consumers; some efficiency-producing deals could be delayed or abandoned, and big transactions would cost more to clear. Those are real but modest compared with the stakes: once a market consolidates, competition is hard to get back. The bill's main weakness is political, not design: it has no Republican support in a Senate where Republicans hold 55 seats, so the likelihood of enactment this Congress is low.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has sat since January 2025 with no hearing, no markup, and no vote, and with no Republican cosponsor it has no clear path to the floor.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 16, 2025, read twice, and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary — the only Senate action it has received.
No committee action, floor vote, or further amendment has been recorded since referral.
All 13 cosponsors are Democrats; no Senate Republican has signed on, and Republicans hold 55 of 100 seats and chair the Judiciary Committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Dominant firms and large acquirers are better off so far, because the current weaker merger standard and enforcement posture remain in place; workers, consumers, and small businesses gain nothing until the bill moves.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Dominant firms, so far — the status quo holds

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.role: U.S. Senator from Minnesota, lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 16, 2025, carrying forward the antitrust reform proposal she first pushed in previous Congresses.

for.name: 13 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including Sens. Whitehouse, Blumenthal, Booker, Hirono, Welch, Heinrich, Markey, Murphy, Smith, Schatz, Warner, Wyden, and Bennet

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (Republican-led)
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican in the 119th Congress
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled in the six months since it arrived.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Majority-party leadership controlling the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Has not signaled interest in bringing antitrust legislation of this kind to the floor, and no Republican has cosponsored the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 13 cosponsors are Democrats; no Senate Republican has signed on, and with Republicans holding 55 seats and chairing the Judiciary Committee, the bill has not received any committee action.

industries.industry: Dominant large corporations across sectors (big tech platforms, national retail and grocery chains, hospital systems, telecom, agribusiness and food processing)
industries.note: The stricter merger standard, monopsony rules, ban on exclusionary conduct, and revenue-based penalties fall hardest on the largest, most concentrated firms, which can currently raise prices and hold down wages with limited antitrust risk. Ordinary consumers and workers are on the opposite side of that trade, so the industry's interest runs against the public's here.

industries.industry: Mergers-and-acquisitions dealmakers (investment banks, law firms, private equity)
industries.note: Burden-of-proof rules for large deals and annual post-deal reporting would make big transactions slower and more expensive to clear, cutting into deal flow and advisory fees.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and companies that rely on arbitration clauses
industries.note: The bill makes pre-dispute arbitration clauses and class-action waivers unenforceable in antitrust disputes, reducing the business of private arbitration firms and ending a tool companies use to keep antitrust claims out of court and away from juries.

industries.industry: Large institutional investors (index funds and asset managers)
industries.note: The bill directs the FTC to study whether institutional investors' overlapping stakes in competitors reduce competition. That is only a study, not a rule, but it could set the stage for future restrictions on common ownership, so the risk is real but the direct impact today is limited.

industries.industry: Antitrust enforcers (DOJ Antitrust Division and FTC)
industries.note: The bill authorizes roughly $1.26 billion in fiscal 2025 funding and lets the agencies keep premerger filing fees, expanding their budgets and staffing well beyond current levels so they can challenge more deals and conduct.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, a Judiciary Committee chaired by a Republican, and no recorded committee action in six months, the bill is unlikely to advance this Congress; Klobuchar's similar proposals in the previous two Congresses likewise stalled in committee, so the realistic path is reintroduction in a future Congress rather than a floor vote now.
